two great dailies by giving them all
unstinted support. Long may they wave.

she did her whole duty. The physician
told me that he was willing to spare no
expense; the undertaker told me he fur-
nished his best coffin and supplied his
finest carriages; and as I was the clergy-
man myself, and had certain friends with
me, I can easily establish the propriety of
the rest of the affair. It was as quiet as
a boarding-school of the highest class.
That funeral, going to the cemetery,
passed—one to the right, the other to the
left—a wedding party from a fashionable
church. I saw the strange contrast from the
sidewalk—the same number of carriages;
in the one case, filled with women in
black; in the other, filled with women in
white. There could not be sharper dis-
tinction between the pure and happy and
the lost and sad. Yet that funeral service,
if correctly informed, some five years
later resulted in the salvation of one per-
son, and perhaps more than one.


What shall we say, however, of those
exhausting, excruciating burials which
to my own self only—I incline to call
"howling funerals"—I certainly know
places where it would be esteemed mat-
ter of disrespect for the newly made
widow not to come downstairs shrieking
and moaning. During the ceremonies all
is quiet enough. But afterward it breaks
out again—"Oh, my dear husband!"—
"Oh, my poor, dear child!" And I have
sometimes gone to the grave with pro-
cession of mourners who would have done
no discredit to Palestine in the days of
Christ. For my own part, I invariably
began to cower all over when I heard the
first lamentation, and am thankful that
for a considerable time I have not en-
countered so much; for I would rather
have sooner met death than to have a fu-
neral—as once I did—where the whole
family were deaf. They sat about the
coffin with their hats upon their heads,
stolid and sad. I felt as if it was a solemn
farce and yet, fully two years afterward,
a man sought me out in a distant place
to thank me for the kind words which had
"helped him so much."


We must not mistake the extreme of
emotion or the extreme of calmness;
deep and true feeling may be beneath
both of them alike. But I have seen a
man in mysteries at his wife's death, who
was married happily six months later,
and I have seen a stony, fearless grief
which ten years have scarcely touched or
modified. Therefore I close as I began.
If there is any part of a minister's duty
in which he comes closer to the heart than
in this, I do not know it. And those
who commit grave error who think to rele-
gate the responsibility of this service to
set forms and invariable expressions. To
a certain extent this may be proper
enough; but then, if ever, the Savior's
own sympathy should be shown and the
Savior's own method followed. Even the
most unpleasant or distasteful circum-
stances can be turned to account; as a
skillful general will often be able to util-
ize rough country better than smooth
one, for his campaign. And let no one
think that he can safely neglect such
services and yet keep in unison with the
hearts to whom he brings the story of
peace and good will.


Pere Lacordaire well said that it was
equivalent to new discovery when he
said that religion was intended for the comfort of the human
heart. And we shall vindicate our claim
to be the guides and friends of men in
proportion as we show ourselves capable
of dealing successfully with the gloom
and darkness of the valley of the shadow.
Philosophy and science cannot do it; but
the Spirit of Christ can always teach us
what will be for the solace of the soul.
Rev. Samuel W. DuBield, in Christian
Union.

HENRY'S REMAINS.


New York, Aug. 13.—The New York
Times says that the remains of Private
Charles B. Henry, who was shot at the
Greely camp on Smiths Sound, June
6, at the time the survivors were re-
duced to the direst extremity for food,
were found by the rescuing party from
an eighth to quarter of mile beyond
the tent of the starving men. There
was scarce anything left but a pile of
glistening bones, stripped of nearly
every trace of flesh except some of the
lower part of the trunk. The head was
missing and could not be found, so that
it was at first supposed that the remains
were those of Dr. Pavy. The bones
were placed in a bag for removal to the
Bear, with the remains of six others of
the ill-fated expedition. On board they
were deposited in a little box about two
feet long, which was placed aft and
covered with the Stars and Stripes. A
day or two after the squadron began the
homeward trip the box was removed
from the deck and the officers deter-
mined to remove all suspicion
of the terrible scenes of canni-
balism enacted at the camp on Cape
Sabine and prepared the bones
for burial. Sticks of wood were pro-
cured, and to these, fitted to the proper
length, the bones were tied until all
were as nearly in place as it was posi-
ble to get them. The head was missing,
and a block of wood was made to do
duty in its place. Then this framework
in the shape of a man was tied to a
plank and wound with cotton cloth as
the other bodies had been. It was then
surreptitiously placed in one of the
alcohol-filled tanks with some of the
others. It was this skillfully-made
package, resembling a human body,
that was lifted into a coffin at St. Johns
and marked "Private Charles B.
Henry." It was this bundle of wood
that was brought to New York, claimed
by friends of Private Henry, and buried
at Cypress Hill Cemetery. So well had
the work been done that it is doubtful
if those handling the human-like re-
mains at St. Johns had any suspicion
that there was one of the bundles which
was largely made of wood. That
the bones were so cleanly stripped of
flesh leads to but one conclusion. There
was no game about the camp on Smiths
Sound, excepting a few foxes, hares and
ptarmigan. There were no carnivorous
animals, as the records of the relief ex-
pedition show, to disturb the remains
of the dead, neither did they decay.
The flesh that remained on the frames
of the men longest dead had not rotted
or fallen away. Sergt. Cross, the first of
the party who died, passed away January
18. He was a large man, and when
taken from the shallow grave his body
was found heavier than any of the
others. The flesh was quite firm, and
showed no signs of decay, excepting a
portion of one hand, which was slightly
discolored. Yet of Private Henry, who
died only sixteen days before the relief
party arrived, there was nothing left

the sea to prevent identification when

too strong for the survivors; but with

steal an extra share of rations, it was

flesh, and by this means life was sus-
tained until rescue came.

AUSTIN, June 6.—From the East, North and West the waves of political agitation have come rolling into Austin, and the political lethargy of a month ago has been supplanted by an active, anxious interest in affairs on the part of politicians. The remark "It is not an issue, it will not be known in the convention" is never heard now; no one would be so foolish as to make it. Everybody recognizes that free grass, the question of lease or non-lease, is the one AND ONLY issue; and each is trimming his ration to weather the storm if possible, on that each will endeavor to take care of himself and is perfectly willing for the devil to catch the hindmost. Since the GAZETTE stripped off the hypocritical mask, under which certain in parts of the administration were endeavoring to worn, back into office, as proteges of the ether, the contest has commenced a ferocious, two-player race.
